specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript introduces Phrasal Recurrent Neural Networks (pRNNs) as a novel architecture designed to explicitly model and utilize task-specific nested phrase structures from plain text in an unsupervised fashion. The core argument is that by representing all potential phrases as fixed-length vectors via an 'RNN pyramid' and selectively combining them with a soft attention mechanism, performance in language modeling and machine translation can be significantly improved. The paper positions this approach as an alternative to relying on human-labeled data for structural information and explores parallel network construction as a design principle. While the architectural components are logically presented and empirical results demonstrate performance gains, the direct validation of the 'unsupervisedly learned phrase structures' themselves remains an area of less explicit focus, and certain experimental setup details raise questions about the direct comparability of results.

P2: Existing methods for incorporating structural information often rely on expensive human-labeled data or external models (Eriguchi et al., 2016; Stahlberg et al., 2016).
C1: Explicitly modeling task-specific nested phrases in an unsupervised manner can enhance NLP task performance (Claim C1, Assumption A3).
M1: The proposed Phrasal Recurrent Neural Network (pRNN) framework is introduced to achieve C1.

S1.1: pRNNs utilize an 'RNN pyramid' (parallel RNNs with shared parameters) to represent phrases of arbitrary lengths as fixed-length vectors (Claim C2, C7). This is presented as an alternative to stacking deeper layers (Claim C6).
S1.2: pRNNs employ a soft attention mechanism to selectively combine candidate phrase suggestions, jointly learned without external knowledge (Claim C3).
S1.3: Computational efficiency is addressed by limiting the candidate phrase set to O(N) (Claim C8).
E1: Empirical validation on Language Modeling (LM) tasks (Penn Treebank, FBIS English) shows over 10 points improvement in perplexity over a state-of-the-art LSTM baseline (Claim C4).
E2: Empirical validation on Machine Translation (MT) tasks (Chinese-English) shows improved BLEU scores over Moses and a strong sequence-to-sequence baseline (Claim C5).
C2: The pRNN model is effective in language modeling and machine translation (Claim C9).
C3: pRNNs represent natural structure in an explicit, human-friendly way (Claim C10).
C4: pRNNs successfully explore parallel network construction as an alternative to deeper layers (Claim C6).
Q1: The quality of the unsupervisedly generated phrase forest, compared to supervised parsing models, remains a significant open question (Assumption A7).

comparable_works.relevance: General context for RNNs in NLP and recursive neural networks.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: This work provides foundational context for neural networks in NLP, including recursive neural networks that explicitly model structure. pRNNs differ by learning structures unsupervisedly and employing a parallel RNN 'pyramid' rather than strictly recursive composition, which often relies on pre-defined parse trees.

comparable_works.citation_label: Linzen et al. (2016)
comparable_works.relevance: Discussion on LSTMs' ability to learn syntax-sensitive dependencies.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: This work suggests that the language modeling signal alone might be insufficient for LSTMs to capture syntax-sensitive dependencies without more direct supervision. pRNNs directly challenge this by demonstrating that unsupervised structural learning, integrated into an RNN, can indeed lead to performance improvements in language modeling, implying that the model *can* leverage structural information without explicit labels.

comparable_works.citation_label: Bahdanau et al. (2014)
comparable_works.relevance: Source of the attention mechanism used in pRNNs.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: The pRNN architecture explicitly adopts the attention mechanism from Bahdanau et al. (2014). The similarity lies in the use of soft attention for weighting inputs. The difference is that pRNNs apply this attention to a 'phrase forest' (representations of all candidate phrases) rather than just individual source words, thereby extending the scope of what the attention mechanism can select from.

comparable_works.citation_label: Eriguchi et al. (2016) and Stahlberg et al. (2016)
comparable_works.relevance: Examples of incorporating structural information with reliance on external resources.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: These works are explicitly cited by the authors as examples of approaches that incorporate structural information (parsing trees, hierarchical phrase-based models) but rely heavily on human-labeled data or external models. pRNNs are presented as a direct counterpoint, aiming to achieve similar benefits without these external dependencies, thus highlighting a key difference in methodology and resource requirements.

alternative_interpretations: The observed performance gains might be primarily attributable to the increased model capacity and the ability of the attention mechanism to select useful features from a richer, multi-scale input space (the 'phrase forest'), rather than a deep, linguistically-grounded understanding of 'nested phrase structures'. The 'parallel network construction' could be interpreted as a form of multi-scale feature extraction, akin to convolutional filters of varying sizes, rather than a fundamentally new dimension of network construction.

The 'task-specific' nature of the learned phrases might be an emergent property of the end-to-end training process, where the model implicitly learns to prioritize phrase representations that are most beneficial for the given task, rather than through an explicit mechanism designed for linguistic specificity.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes Phrasal Recurrent Neural Networks (pRNNs) as a novel architecture to explicitly model and utilize task-specific nested phrase structures from plain text in an unsupervised manner. The core methodological innovation lies in the 'RNN pyramid' which generates fixed-length vector representations for all possible continuous phrases of arbitrary lengths within a sentence. A soft attention mechanism is then employed to selectively combine these candidate phrase suggestions when predicting the next word or encoding a source sentence. The authors claim that this approach, by providing explicit structural information, leads to significant performance improvements in language modeling (perplexity) and machine translation (BLEU score) over state-of-the-art LSTM and sequence-to-sequence baselines. Furthermore, the architecture explores parallel network construction as an alternative to stacking deeper layers, with parameter sharing across the parallel RNNs to maintain consistency and limit complexity. The evaluation setup involves standard datasets and metrics, comparing pRNNs against established baselines, but some aspects of the experimental methodology raise concerns regarding the fairness and robustness of these comparisons.

concerns.title: Lack of Explicit Evaluation for Learned Phrase Structures
concerns.description: A core claim is that pRNNs 'effectively models task-specific nested phrases from plain text in an unsupervised manner.' However, the paper does not provide any explicit qualitative or quantitative evaluation of the quality or interpretability of these learned phrase structures (the 'phrase forest'). The authors themselves acknowledge this as a 'significant question that remains.' Without such an evaluation, it is difficult to ascertain *what* structures are being learned and if they are linguistically meaningful or merely statistical artifacts that happen to improve task performance.
evidence: The proposed Phrasal Recurrent Neural Network (pRNN) framework effectively models task-specific nested phrases from plain text in an unsupervised manner.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include an analysis of the learned phrase structures. This could involve visualizing attention weights, extracting high-scoring phrases, or comparing the induced 'phrase forest' to gold-standard parse trees (even if not used for training) using metrics like F1 score for phrase detection or structural similarity measures. specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript introduces Phrasal Recurrent Neural Networks (pRNNs), a novel architectural framework designed to explicitly model and utilize task-specific nested phrase structures from plain text in an unsupervised manner. The core innovation lies in the 'RNN pyramid,' a parallel arrangement of shifted RNN sequences that generates fixed-length vector representations for all potential phrases (a 'phrase forest'). A soft attention mechanism then dynamically selects and combines these phrase representations to inform subsequent predictions in tasks like language modeling and machine translation. This approach diverges from traditional methods that either rely on explicit, human-labeled parsing trees or implicitly learn sequential dependencies. The authors also present pRNNs as an exploration of 'parallel network construction' as an alternative to the common practice of stacking deeper RNN layers. Empirical results demonstrate significant performance improvements, including over 10 points perplexity reduction in language modeling and improved BLEU scores in machine translation, over strong state-of-the-art baselines.
logical_argument_graph: Natural language contains latent nested structures beyond simple word sequences, which, if effectively modeled, can enhance NLP task performance (Chomsky, 1957).
Existing methods for incorporating structural information often depend on expensive human-labeled data (e.g., parsing trees) or external models, limiting their applicability and scalability.

Hypothesis: An RNN architecture capable of explicitly and *unsupervisedly* discovering and utilizing task-specific nested phrase structures will yield superior performance in language modeling and machine translation.
Proposed Solution (pRNN): A novel framework comprising three interacting subnetworks: Phrasal part (P), Attention part (A), and Sequential part (S).

Mechanism 1 (Phrase Representation - P): The 'RNN pyramid' (parallel, shifted RNNs with shared parameters) is constructed to generate fixed-length vector representations for all potential phrases within a sentence, forming a 'phrase forest' (C2, C7). This allows for representing phrases of arbitrary lengths.

Mechanism 2 (Phrase Utilization - A): A soft attention mechanism dynamically selects and combines the most relevant candidate phrase representations from the 'phrase forest' at each time step (C3). This process is jointly learned with the task objective, eliminating the need for external knowledge on chunking or composition (C1).

Mechanism 3 (Sequential Integration - S): The weighted sum of selected phrases (from A) is integrated into the conventional RNN sequence, allowing the model to incorporate structural history information into its hidden state for next-word prediction (Section 2).
Architectural Philosophy: The pRNN architecture implicitly explores 'parallel network construction' as a novel dimension for building neural networks, distinct from stacking deeper layers (C6).
Evaluation: The pRNN model is empirically tested on established language modeling (Penn Treebank, FBIS English) and machine translation (Chinese-English) tasks.
Results (LM): pRNNs achieve significant perplexity improvements (over 10 points) compared to a state-of-the-art LSTM baseline (C4).
Results (MT): pRNNs demonstrate improved BLEU scores over both a phrase-based statistical machine translation (Moses) and a strong sequence-to-sequence neural machine translation baseline (C5).

Conclusion: The pRNN model is effective in language modeling and machine translation, demonstrating the utility of its novel approach to unsupervised, explicit structural modeling and parallel network construction (C9). The approach aims for explicit, 'human-friendly' structure representation (C10).

The manuscript introduces Phrasal Recurrent Neural Networks (pRNNs), a novel architectural framework designed to explicitly model and utilize task-specific nested phrase structures from plain text in an unsupervised manner. A soft attention mechanism then dynamically selects and combines these phrase representations to inform subsequent predictions in tasks like language modeling and machine translation. This approach diverges from traditional methods that either rely on explicit, human-labeled parsing trees or implicitly learn sequential dependencies. The authors also present pRNNs as an exploration of 'parallel network construction' as an alternative to the common practice of stacking deeper RNN layers. Empirical results demonstrate significant performance improvements, including over 10 points perplexity reduction in language modeling and improved BLEU scores in machine translation, over strong state-of-the-art baselines.

consensus_findings: The proposed Phrasal Recurrent Neural Network (pRNN) framework introduces a novel architectural approach for explicitly modeling and utilizing task-specific nested phrase structures from plain text in an unsupervised manner (Claims C1, C2).

The 'RNN pyramid' component, which represents phrases of arbitrary lengths as fixed-length vectors, and the exploration of parallel network construction as an alternative to stacking deeper layers, are recognized as significant architectural innovations (Claims C2, C6).
The pRNN framework employs a soft attention mechanism to selectively combine candidate phrase suggestions (Claim C3).

The paper provides strong empirical evidence of significant performance improvements in language modeling tasks, achieving over 10 points improvement in perplexity on Penn Treebank and FBIS English datasets compared to a state-of-the-art LSTM baseline (Claim C4).
The paper reports improvements in BLEU scores for Chinese-English machine translation over both Moses and a strong sequence-to-sequence baseline (Claim C5).

The design incorporates parameter sharing across parallel RNNs in the pyramid and a reduction of the candidate phrase set from O(N^2) to O(N), contributing to computational efficiency and parameter economy (Claims C7, C8).
The problem statement and motivation for unsupervised structural learning are clearly articulated.
disagreements: Reviewers hold differing perspectives on the *type* of novelty presented: one novelty assessor (R3) views the contribution as 'Incremental but Meaningful,' building upon existing RNN and attention paradigms, while another (R4) identifies 'High novelty,' potentially 'disruptive,' particularly regarding the 'parallel network construction' and the conceptual framework for unsupervised structural learning. A claim verifier (R5) supports incremental novelty and partially supports disruptive novelty, noting that the disruptive impact is yet to be fully realized.

There is a controlled disagreement on the *severity* of the methodological flaw concerning the machine translation baseline comparison. The methodology auditor (R2) rates it as 'major' due to its impact on validity and reproducibility, while other reviewers (R1, R3, R5) rate it as 'moderate,' and the disruptive novelty assessor (R4) rates it as 'minor,' noting its impact on the strength of evidence for disruptive novelty rather than the novelty itself.
uncertainty_hotspots: The quality and linguistic meaningfulness of the unsupervisedly learned phrase structures are not explicitly evaluated or compared to supervised methods, leaving the 'effectively models' and 'human-friendly' aspects of claims C1 and C10 partially unsubstantiated beyond downstream task performance.

The scalability and discriminative power of the soft attention mechanism, especially when dealing with a large number of complex candidate phrases, are questioned by the authors themselves and highlighted by all reviewers as a potential limitation (Claim C3).

The fairness and robustness of the machine translation baseline comparison are uncertain due to the explicit statement that the baseline (RNNsearch) was run 'many times' to report the best result, while the proposed pRNN model was run 'only once' (Claim C5).
The precise mechanism by which the learned phrases become 'task-specific' beyond being optimized for the end task is not explicitly detailed.
The impact of full parameter sharing across all parallel RNNs in the pyramid on the model's representational capacity for diverse phrase types is a minor area of uncertainty.
The robustness of performance gains to different hyperparameter choices (e.g., dropout rate chosen 'without tuning') is not fully explored.
model_diversity_effects: The `structure_analyst` (R1) provided a foundational understanding of the paper's logical coherence, highlighting architectural strengths and logical gaps like the lack of direct structure evaluation.
The `methodology_auditor` (R2) rigorously scrutinized experimental validity, identifying the unequal MT baseline comparison as a 'major' flaw and emphasizing reproducibility concerns.

The `novelty_assessor_incremental` (R3) and `novelty_assessor_disruptive` (R4) roles collectively offered a comprehensive view of the paper's innovation, distinguishing between incremental advancements and potentially paradigm-shifting ideas like 'parallel network construction.' R4's dual perspective (incremental and disruptive) was particularly insightful.

The `claim_verifier` (R5) systematically mapped claims to evidence and uncertainties, providing a detailed and evidence-based assessment of the support for each claim, reinforcing the critical concerns raised by other roles.

The combination of roles ensured a multi-faceted evaluation, covering logical soundness, empirical rigor, and different dimensions of scientific contribution, leading to a balanced synthesis of strengths and weaknesses.
meta_review.editor_guidance: The paper presents a novel and architecturally innovative approach with strong empirical results in language modeling. The core architectural ideas, particularly the 'RNN pyramid' and 'parallel network construction,' are widely recognized as significant contributions. However, the methodological concern regarding the fairness of the machine translation baseline comparison is substantial and needs to be addressed for the MT results to be fully credible. Furthermore, the consistent lack of direct evaluation of the unsupervisedly learned phrase structures is a critical gap in substantiating the paper's central claim of 'effectively modeling' linguistic structures. The editor should weigh the robust language modeling performance and architectural novelty against these significant methodological and validation concerns, particularly for the MT task and the interpretability of the learned structures.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript, authors should: 1) Re-run machine translation experiments ensuring equivalent rigor (e.g., multiple runs, consistent hyperparameter tuning) for both the proposed pRNN model and all baselines, reporting average performance and standard deviations. 2) Include a dedicated section for qualitative and/or quantitative analysis of the unsupervisedly learned phrase structures, perhaps by visualizing attention weights, extracting representative phrases, or comparing induced structures to gold-standard parses. This would provide direct evidence for the 'modeling' and 'human-friendly' claims. 3) Further investigate the behavior and limitations of the soft attention mechanism, especially with varying sentence lengths and phrase complexities, and consider exploring more sophisticated attention strategies. 4) Conduct a limited sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters (e.g., dropout rate) to demonstrate the robustness of the performance gains. 5) Elaborate on how the joint learning process specifically induces 'task-specific' properties in the learned phrase representations.

human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: The paper presents a novel and architecturally innovative approach with strong empirical results in language modeling. The core architectural ideas, particularly the 'RNN pyramid' and 'parallel network construction,' are widely recognized as significant contributions. However, the methodological concern regarding the fairness of the machine translation baseline comparison is substantial and needs to be addressed for the MT results to be fully credible. Furthermore, the consistent lack of direct evaluation of the unsupervisedly learned phrase structures is a critical gap in substantiating the paper's central claim of 'effectively modeling' linguistic structures. The editor should weigh the robust language modeling performance and architectural novelty against these significant methodological and validation concerns, particularly for the MT task and the interpretability of the learned structures.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript, authors should: 1) Re-run machine translation experiments ensuring equivalent rigor (e.g., multiple runs, consistent hyperparameter tuning) for both the proposed pRNN model and all baselines, reporting average performance and standard deviations. 2) Include a dedicated section for qualitative and/or quantitative analysis of the unsupervisedly learned phrase structures, perhaps by visualizing attention weights, extracting representative phrases, or comparing induced structures to gold-standard parses. This would provide direct evidence for the 'modeling' and 'human-friendly' claims. 3) Further investigate the behavior and limitations of the soft attention mechanism, especially with varying sentence lengths and phrase complexities, and consider exploring more sophisticated attention strategies. 4) Conduct a limited sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters (e.g., dropout rate) to demonstrate the robustness of the performance gains. 5) Elaborate on how the joint learning process specifically induces 'task-specific' properties in the learned phrase representations.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The paper introduces Phrasal Recurrent Neural Networks (pRNNs), a novel architecture that explicitly models and utilizes task-specific nested phrase structures from plain text in an unsupervised manner. This is achieved through an 'RNN pyramid' for fixed-length phrase vector representation and a soft attention mechanism for selective phrase combination. The architecture also explores parallel network construction as an alternative to stacking deeper layers. The work demonstrates significant performance improvements in language modeling (perplexity) and machine translation (BLEU scores) over strong baselines, though concerns exist regarding the direct evaluation of learned structures and the fairness of some experimental comparisons.

Strengths:
- The proposed Phrasal Recurrent Neural Network (pRNN) framework introduces a novel architectural approach for explicitly modeling and utilizing task-specific nested phrase structures from plain text in an unsupervised manner.
- The 'RNN pyramid' component, which represents phrases of arbitrary lengths as fixed-length vectors, and the exploration of parallel network construction as an alternative to stacking deeper layers, are recognized as significant architectural innovations.
- The pRNN framework employs a soft attention mechanism to selectively combine candidate phrase suggestions.
- The paper provides strong empirical evidence of significant performance improvements in language modeling tasks, achieving over 10 points improvement in perplexity on Penn Treebank and FBIS English datasets compared to a state-of-the-art LSTM baseline.
- The paper reports improvements in BLEU scores for Chinese-English machine translation over both Moses (phrase-based statistical model) and a strong sequence-to-sequence baseline.
- The design incorporates parameter sharing across parallel RNNs in the pyramid and a reduction of the candidate phrase set from O(N^2) to O(N), contributing to computational efficiency and parameter economy.
- The problem statement and motivation for unsupervised structural learning are clearly articulated.

Limitations:
- The paper claims to effectively model task-specific nested phrases and represent natural structure in an explicit, human-friendly way, but provides no direct qualitative or quantitative analysis of these learned structures. The effectiveness of unsupervised phrase learning is inferred solely from downstream task performance, leaving the quality and interpretability of the generated 'phrase forest' unverified.
- The experimental setup for machine translation explicitly states that the baseline (RNNsearch) was run 'many times' to report the best result, while the proposed pRNN model was run 'only once.' This unequal optimization effort significantly undermines the fairness and robustness of the reported BLEU score improvements, potentially overstating the pRNN's advantage in MT.
- The scalability and discriminative power of the soft attention mechanism, especially when dealing with a large number of complex candidate phrases, are questioned by the authors themselves and highlighted by reviewers as a potential limitation.
- The mechanism by which the learned phrases become 'task-specific' beyond simply being optimized for the end task is not explicitly detailed, raising questions about the depth of linguistic specificity.
- The robustness of performance gains to different hyperparameter choices (e.g., dropout rate chosen 'without tuning') is not fully explored, potentially affecting the generalizability of the results.

Open Questions:
- How do the unsupervisedly learned phrase structures qualitatively and quantitatively compare to linguistically motivated structures from supervised parsing models? Can examples of these 'human-friendly' structures be visualized or analyzed to provide direct evidence of their quality and interpretability?
- What is the behavior of the attention mechanism with varying sentence lengths and phrase complexities? Can more sophisticated attention mechanisms or hierarchical attention strategies improve its discriminative power and scalability for large candidate sets?
- Can the authors provide a more detailed explanation of how the joint learning process specifically induces 'task-specific' properties in the learned phrase representations?
- What is the impact of full parameter sharing across all parallel RNNs in the pyramid on the model's representational capacity for diverse phrase types? Would partial sharing or independent parameters offer benefits?

- The paper clearly states the definition of 'phrase' adopted from PBSMT, which is helpful for understanding the scope of the structural units being modeled.

The rapid adoption of RNNs in NLP systems in recent years, in particular of RNNs with gating mecha- nisms such as long short-term memory (LSTM) units (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) or gated recur- rent units (GRU) (Cho et al., 2014), has led to sig- niﬁcant gains in language modeling (Mikolov et al., 2010; Sundermeyer et al., 2012), parsing (Vinyals et al., 2015; Kiperwasser and Goldberg, 2016; Dyer et al., 2016), machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015) and other tasks. The effectiveness of RNNs1 is attributed to their ability to capture statistical contingencies that may span an arbitrary number of words. The wordFrance, for example, is more likely to occur somewhere in a sentence that begins with Paris than in a sentence that begins with Penguins. The fact that an arbitrary number of words can intervene between the mutually predictive words implies that they cannot be captured by models with a ﬁxed window such asn-gram mod- els, but can in principle be captured by RNNs, which do not have an architecturally ﬁxed limit on depen- dency length.

These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 5. Check that your scores reflect the review I3
Codes: I3
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

Section: 5. Check that your scores reflect the review I3
Codes: I3
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation. I3 The soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review . If you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, this means that your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation, and you need to revise it. One possible reason for low soundness scores without sufficient justification could be reliance on some unconscious bias or heuristic, like the ones listed in the previous section. Likewise, low reproducibility scores should be justified. Sometimes you may find the work sound, but not something that is interesting for you personally. Such preferences are more subjective and should be reflected in a separate excitement score, which is orthogonal to the assessment of the soundness of the paper. Excitement scores reflect our personal taste, and so do not necessarily come with explicit reasons. The Overall assessment score is an explicit recommendation for the outcome of this paper, if it were committed to an *ACL venue. This is a composite score reflecting your assessment of soundness, excitement, and also other factors like novelty and impact. All papers recommended for Findings and main conferences are expected to be sufficiently sound and reproducible, but you may consider a paper worthy of the main conference even if you personally are not excited about it.

The rapid adoption of RNNs in NLP systems in recent years, in particular of RNNs with gating mecha- nisms such as long short-term memory (LSTM) units (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) or gated recur- rent units (GRU) (Cho et al., 2014), has led to sig- niﬁcant gains in language modeling (Mikolov et al., 2010; Sundermeyer et al., 2012), parsing (Vinyals et al., 2015; Kiperwasser and Goldberg, 2016; Dyer et al., 2016), machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015) and other tasks. The effectiveness of RNNs1 is attributed to their ability to capture statistical contingencies that may span an arbitrary number of words. The wordFrance, for example, is more likely to occur somewhere in a sentence that begins with Paris than in a sentence that begins with Penguins. The fact that an arbitrary number of words can intervene between the mutually predictive words implies that they cannot be captured by models with a ﬁxed window such asn-gram mod- els, but can in principle be captured by RNNs, which do not have an architecturally ﬁxed limit on depen- dency length.

Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Codes: I1, I12

Content: eview earlier and ask more experienced people in your network for feedback. Some ACs may also offer feedback for reviews that come in good time. Irresponsible reviewers and chairs. Unfortunately, with the growing number of conference submissions, there have been more and more cases where reviewers or chairs sign up for service and then simply disappear without a warning, are late without a warning, or submit (meta-)reviews that are completely unacceptable in their quality (e.g. extremely terse, unprofessional in tone, LLM-generated). Starting in October 2024, ARR provided the authors with the opportunity to report common issues with reviews (e.g. rude reviews, ‘not novel’ criticism without providing references, etc.) The ACs will see such reports, if any, judge their merit, and take them into account when writing the meta-review. A similar functionality has now been developed for meta-reviews, with author issue reports viewable for senior area chairs. Since the reviewer and AC guidelines may also seen by the authors during the response period, some sections of these guidelines now have codes for (meta-)review issues (I1-I12) that can be reported by the authors. More details here and here. Starting in May 2025, ARR also adopts the new policy on the ‘highly irresponsible’ (meta-)reviewers. The program chairs and ARR EiCs will consider the egregious cases reported by chairs (on their own judgement or based on author reports), including the cases of extremely terse reviews, unprofessional tone, and LLM-generated reviews.

Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Section: 🆕 ACL policy on great and irresponsible reviewers & chairs
Codes: I1, I12
Applies To: meta_reviewer, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, policy_screen, structure_analyst
Content: eview earlier and ask more experienced people in your network for feedback. Some ACs may also offer feedback for reviews that come in good time. Irresponsible reviewers and chairs. Unfortunately, with the growing number of conference submissions, there have been more and more cases where reviewers or chairs sign up for service and then simply disappear without a warning, are late without a warning, or submit (meta-)reviews that are completely unacceptable in their quality (e.g. extremely terse, unprofessional in tone, LLM-generated). Starting in October 2024, ARR provided the authors with the opportunity to report common issues with reviews (e.g. rude reviews, ‘not novel’ criticism without providing references, etc.) The ACs will see such reports, if any, judge their merit, and take them into account when writing the meta-review. A similar functionality has now been developed for meta-reviews, with author issue reports viewable for senior area chairs. Since the reviewer and AC guidelines may also seen by the authors during the response period, some sections of these guidelines now have codes for (meta-)review issues (I1-I12) that can be reported by the authors. More details here and here. Starting in May 2025, ARR also adopts the new policy on the ‘highly irresponsible’ (meta-)reviewers. The program chairs and ARR EiCs will consider the egregious cases reported by chairs (on their own judgement or based on author reports), including the cases of extremely terse reviews, unprofessional tone, and LLM-generated reviews.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

The rapid adoption of RNNs in NLP systems in recent years, in particular of RNNs with gating mecha- nisms such as long short-term memory (LSTM) units (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) or gated recur- rent units (GRU) (Cho et al., 2014), has led to sig- niﬁcant gains in language modeling (Mikolov et al., 2010; Sundermeyer et al., 2012), parsing (Vinyals et al., 2015; Kiperwasser and Goldberg, 2016; Dyer et al., 2016), machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2015) and other tasks. The effectiveness of RNNs1 is attributed to their ability to capture statistical contingencies that may span an arbitrary number of words. The wordFrance, for example, is more likely to occur somewhere in a sentence that begins with Paris than in a sentence that begins with Penguins. The fact that an arbitrary number of words can intervene between the mutually predictive words implies that they cannot be captured by models with a ﬁxed window such asn-gram mod- els, but can in principle be captured by RNNs, which do not have an architecturally ﬁxed limit on depen- dency length.

These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
